sense: what matters in what is said
also: but to return to the point

terms.gloss: the matter in hand, the point
terms.grammar: noun, fifth declension: ad rem, to the point; nihil ad rem, beside the point
evidence: Ter. Ad. 2.1.31: mitte ista, atque ad rem redī (Lewis & Short s.v. redeō)
Cic. Caecin. 58: nihil ad rem pertinet (Lewis & Short s.v. ad)
Traupman 105: beside the point; get to the point!; get the point?, nihil ad rem; venī ad rem!; tenēsne rem?
terms.comment: English “the point” is Latin rēs, the matter itself: ad rem redī, get back to the point; nihil ad rem, nothing to do with the matter; tenēsne rem?, do you follow?

terms.grammar: in id caput est, quod caput est: that is the main point, the main thing is
evidence: Cic. Att. 1.17.4: id quod caput est
Traupman 105: that’s the main point, id caput est
Traupman 106: the point is that I no longer care about such things, quod caput est, jam ista nōn cūrō

terms.gloss: the subject in hand: back to the point
evidence: Cic. Div. 2.79: sed lābor longius; ad prōpositum revertor (Lewis & Short s.v. lābor)
Traupman 105: but to return to the point …, sed ad prōpositum …

terms.gloss: up to this point, so far
evidence: Hor. S. 1.4.63: hāctenus haec (Lewis & Short s.v. alius)
Traupman 105: up to this point, hāctenus
terms.comment: Very frequent in Cicero, Lewis & Short notes, to mark where a topic ends: hāctenus haec, so much for that.

terms.gloss: it came to the point where
terms.grammar: impersonal passive of dēcurrō, with eō, “to that point”
evidence: Liv. 26.18: postrēmō eō dēcursum est, ut … (Lewis & Short s.v. dēcurrō)
Traupman 105: it got to the point where, eō dēcursum est ut (+ subj.)

phrases.latin: Mitte ista, atque ad rem redī.
phrases.english: Drop all that and get back to the point.
What’s your point? (What are you driving at?)

phrases.latin: Quid rētulit tē mittere ad mē litterās?
phrases.english: What was the point of your writing to me?

sources: Lewis & Short: res · Lewis & Short: propositum · Lewis & Short: hactenus · Lewis & Short: decurro
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 104–106, each phrase checked against the searchable text of the book.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
